claim: Sudden peripheral motion amplifies and accelerates information transmission in salamander ganglion cells in a 50 ms time window.
source: Here, we show that sudden peripheral motion amplifies and accelerates information transmission in salamander ganglion cells in a 50 ms time window.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-4 showing increased information transmission during a specific time window after peripheral stimulation.

claim: A transient increase in adaptation to contrast underlies the gating of information by peripheral motion.
source: Underlying this gating of information is a transient increase in adaptation to contrast, enhancing sensitivity to a broader range of stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing changes in adaptation index and nonlinearity slopes at different contrasts during the gating window.

claim: The effect of peripheral gating coincides with an expected increase in information in bipolar cells after a global image shift.
source: Using a model and natural images, we show that this effect coincides with an expected increase in information in bipolar cells after a global image shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results presented in Figure 7, which compares the timing of gating with expected information increases from natural image shifts.

claim: Peripheral stimulation enhances sensitivity to weak central stimuli during abrupt global image motion.
source: Thus, peripheral stimulation enhanced the sensitivity to weak central stimuli during abrupt global image motion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing increased firing rate slopes as a function of central luminance during global shifts compared to object shifts.

claim: Cells with the weakest response to the object condition showed the greatest enhancement of sensitivity from peripheral motion.
source: In doing so, we found that the cells with the weakest response to the object condition showed the greatest enhancement of sensitivity from peripheral motion, with 39 out of 76 cells at least doubling the slope of their firing rate vs. the log of central luminance (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D showing the relationship between baseline firing rate and enhancement ratio.

claim: The increased activity during the global shift condition could not be attributed to the linear receptive field of the cell overlapping the object border.
source: This increased activity during the global shift condition could not be attributed to the linear receptive field of the cell overlapping the object border, as steps to the right and left would have linear contributions of opposite signs, even if such stimuli might be within the spatial region occupied by the classical receptive field surround (Demb et al., 2001; Borghuis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by logical inference from the experimental design and cited literature on receptive field properties.

claim: The effect of the global shift was mostly insensitive to the phase of the checkers in the periphery.
source: Accordingly, the effect of the global shift was mostly insensitive to the phase of the checkers in the periphery (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 2B inset, where both phases of peripheral shifts produce similar effects.

claim: Shortly after peripheral stimulation there was an excitatory effect indicated by an increase in firing.
source: For most recorded cells, shortly after peripheral stimulation there was an excitatory effect – indicated by an increase in firing (Krüger and Fischer, 1973) – followed by strong inhibition as might underlie a previously reported component of saccadic suppression (Roska and Werblin, 2003), and then a slower recovery to the baseline state (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and cited previous literature on peripheral excitation.

claim: Peripheral excitation is followed by strong inhibition that may underlie saccadic suppression.
source: For most recorded cells, shortly after peripheral stimulation there was an excitatory effect – indicated by an increase in firing (Krüger and Fischer, 1973) – followed by strong inhibition as might underlie a previously reported component of saccadic suppression (Roska and Werblin, 2003), and then a slower recovery to the baseline state (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and cited literature on saccadic suppression mechanisms.

claim: The temporal filter changed little during the gating window compared to the still condition.
source: Even though the firing rate greatly increased during 50–100 ms after the peripheral shift, the temporal filter changed little when compared to the still condition, indicating that the cell continued to convey the same average feature about the visual stimulus during the 50 ms high firing rate interval (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C comparing linear filters under different conditions.

claim: The sensitivity to the central stimulus was greatest 50–100 ms after a peripheral shift.
source: We defined the sensitivity to the central stimulus as the average slope of the nonlinearity (Kastner and Baccus, 2011; Baccus and Meister, 2002) and found that the sensitivity was the greatest 50–100 ms after a peripheral shift, during the high firing rate window.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing nonlinearity slopes at different times relative to peripheral shifts.

claim: An abrupt peripheral shift dynamically gates the response of a cell, enhancing the cell's sensitivity to its preferred visual feature near the receptive field center.
source: Instead, we find that an abrupt peripheral shift dynamically gates the response of a cell, enhancing the cell's sensitivity to its preferred visual feature near the receptive field center.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the LN model analysis and data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Just after a peripheral shift, information about the central stimulus sharply increased as compared to when the periphery was still.
source: We found that just after a peripheral shift, information about the central stimulus sharply increased as compared to when the periphery was still, indicating that a signal from the periphery increases information transmission from the central region (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by mutual information calculations presented in Figure 2D.

claim: All cell types showed a sharp increase of information during the gating window, with the peak time depending on the cell type.
source: All cell types showed a sharp increase of information during the gating window, with the peak time depending on the cell type (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2E showing information dynamics for different cell types.

claim: After a shift, the information conveyed was 0.47 ± 0.04 of the maximal value, compared with 0.24 ± 0.05 before the shift.
source: After a shift, the information conveyed was 0.47 ± 0.04, (n = 18 cells) of the maximal value, compared with 0.24 ± 0.05 before the shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations comparing actual information transmission to theoretical maximum based on noise properties.

claim: After the shift, the neural code used more of the capacity of the cell given its noise properties and the spike count code.
source: Thus, after the shift, the neural code used more of the capacity of the cell given its noise properties and the spike count code.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of actual to maximal information transmission values.

claim: The increased information transmission came at the increased cost of energy in terms of a higher firing rate.
source: However, this came at the increased cost of energy in terms of a higher firing rate (6.9 ± 1.7 Hz after the shift, and 1.9 ± 0.3 before the shift).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurements of firing rates before and after peripheral shifts.

claim: After a peripheral shift, the neural code shifts away from energy conservation and towards high-throughput information transmission.
source: Our analysis indicates that after a peripheral shift, the neural code shifts away from energy conservation and towards high-throughput information transmission.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the analysis of information transmission efficiency and firing rates.

claim: Both excitation and inhibition from a peripheral shift depended on the central contrast, with a much stronger increase in firing observed at low contrast.
source: We observed that both excitation and inhibition from a peripheral shift depended on the central contrast, with a much stronger increase in firing observed at low contrast (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing PSTHs at different contrasts.

claim: Peripheral stimulation affected the sensitivity, but had a minimal effect on the average local features preferred by the ganglion cells.
source: Thus, peripheral stimulation affected the sensitivity, but had a minimal effect on the average local features preferred by the ganglion cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of temporal filters at different contrasts shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the gating window, responses to different contrasts were much more similar to each other, indicating a greater level of adaptation to the central contrast.
source: We found that in the gating window, responses to different contrasts were much more similar to each other, indicating a greater level of adaptation to the central contrast (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C showing nonlinearities at different contrasts during different time windows.

claim: At 3% contrast, the slope changed by 5.5 ± 1.1 Hz per contrast unit and at 24% contrast the slope changed by 0.20 ± 0.06 Hz per contrast unit.
source: At 3% contrast, the slope changed by 5.5 ± 1.1 Hz per contrast unit (one s.d. of the nonlinearity input was 0.03 contrast units, or 3% ) and at 24% contrast the slope changed by 0.20 ± 0.06 Hz per contrast unit (one s.d. was 0.24 contrast units, or 24% ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim provides specific quantitative measurements from the experimental data.

claim: Most cells increased their adaptation to contrast during the gating window, such that all contrasts were represented with more similar responses than during the recovery window.
source: We computed an index of adaptation that takes the value of 1 for an ideally adapting cell and 0 for a non-adapting cell (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), and found that most cells increased their adaptation to contrast during the gating window, such that all contrasts were represented with more similar responses than during the recovery window (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the adaptation index calculations presented in Figure 3D.

claim: An increase in adaptation underlies the increase in information during the gating window, such that near the receptive field center, both weak and strong signals are conveyed.
source: This indicates that an increase in adaptation underlies the increase in information during the gating window, such that near the receptive field center, both weak and strong signals are conveyed.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the adaptation analysis and information measurements.

claim: The responses coming from the same cell at different times carry different types of information.
source: We found that the responses coming from the same cell at different times carry different types of information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis in Figure 4C showing different dynamics for sequence and contrast information.

claim: A dynamic neural code avoids the tradeoff between adaptation and preserving the adapting statistic by rapidly switching between complementary representations of the same stimulus.
source: Whereas a static neural code would typically face the choice between adaptation and preserving the adapting statistic, a dynamic neural code avoids this tradeoff by rapidly switching between complementary representations of the same stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observation that sequence and contrast information are encoded at different times.

claim: The model effectively replicated the data for Gaussian stimuli at different contrasts.
source: The model effectively replicated the data for Gaussian stimuli at different contrasts (Figure 5C, D), as well as for constant luminance stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model outputs to experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Because the peripheral input is delivered prior to the threshold and adaptive stage, it is summed with the unadapted measure of the central input.
source: Because the peripheral input is delivered prior to the threshold and adaptive stage, it is summed with the unadapted measure of the central input.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The peripheral input has a larger effect on weak central stimuli than on strong ones.
source: This causes the peripheral input to have a larger effect on weak central stimuli than on strong ones as experimentally observed (Figures 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that matches experimental observations.

claim: Weak stimuli only cross threshold when peripheral input is applied.
source: Furthermore, weak stimuli only cross threshold when peripheral input is applied (Figure 5B), allowing the adaptive stage to encode and adapt to signals of all strengths, including those from a central stimulus with a constant intensity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A single amplitude of peripheral input replicates the results at all central contrasts.
source: An important conclusion we derived from the model is that a single amplitude of peripheral input (equivalent to a fixed threshold shift with respect to the central input) replicates the results at all central contrasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis showing that contrast-dependent effects arise from adaptation, not from the peripheral signal itself.

claim: The peripheral signal itself delivered prior to the threshold does not depend on the central contrast.
source: Thus even though the effects of peripheral input differ with the central contrast, this is because of the differing downstream effects of adaptation; the peripheral signal itself delivered prior to the threshold does not depend on the central contrast.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure and its ability to replicate data with a fixed peripheral input amplitude.

claim: The excitatory influence of gating acted at distances of up to 1 mm.
source: The excitatory influence of gating acted at distances of up to 1 mm (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of sensitivity as a function of distance shown in Figure 6.

claim: The observed changes in sensitivity indicate that excitatory and inhibitory influences acted over a similar scale, equivalent to a radius of ~20 deg. of visual angle.
source: The observed changes in sensitivity indicate that excitatory and inhibitory influences acted over a similar scale, equivalent to a radius of ~20 deg. of visual angle.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial extent measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Global image shifts generate a signal that increases information transfer about a cell's preferred visual feature from local regions near the receptive field center.
source: Our results show that global image shifts generate a signal that increases information transfer about a cell's preferred visual feature from local regions near the receptive field center.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the gating time window, a change in the neural code is explained by a simple additive signal prior to a threshold followed by an adaptive stage.
source: In the gating time window, a change in the neural code is explained by a simple additive signal prior to a threshold followed by an adaptive stage.
evidence: This is supported by the model presented in Figure 5 that successfully replicates experimental observations.

claim: A broader range of signals is transmitted after peripheral stimulation, with a stronger effect on weak, low-contrast stimuli commonly found in natural scenes.
source: As a result, a broader range of signals is transmitted, with a stronger effect on weak, low-contrast stimuli commonly found in natural scenes (Tadmor and Tolhurst, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing greater effects at low contrast and cited literature on natural scene statistics.

claim: The gating of information transmission resolves two competing needs: conservation of spikes and the rapid encoding of information when it is expected that information in the center will suddenly increase.
source: We explain the functional importance of this effect as the resolution of two competing needs: conservation of spikes and the rapid encoding of information when it is expected that information in the center will suddenly increase.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The statistics over the receptive field center depend both on the image and the sequence of eye movements, and have strong correlations over time.
source: The statistics over the receptive field center depend both on the image and the sequence of eye movements, and have strong correlations over time.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about natural image statistics and eye movements.

claim: Fast Off-type bipolar cells are roughly linear at a constant mean intensity for a stimulus that flickers or jitters as in fixational eye movements.
source: Fast Off-type bipolar cells are roughly linear at a constant mean intensity for a stimulus that flickers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) or jitters as in fixational eye movements, and previous models indicate that these cells may convey the primary input to fast Off-type ganglion cells (Baccus et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and cited previous work.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio in bipolar cells increased with contrast.
source: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) increased with contrast, which was incorporated into the model ( Figure 7A-iii, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7A-iii.

claim: During a brief window of time after the shift, the light intensity seen by the bipolar cell was less correlated with its previous values.
source: However, for a brief window of time after the shift, the light intensity seen by the bipolar cell was less correlated with its previous values (Figure 7B, D and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: After the sudden shift moved the receptive field to a new location, the conditional mutual information abruptly increased.
source: However, after the sudden shift moved the receptive field to a new location, the conditional mutual information abruptly increased (Figure 7C, solid line).
evidence: This is shown by information calculations from the model presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The conditional mutual information showed faster dynamics, with new information arriving faster than the peak of the linear prediction.
source: Most importantly, the conditional mutual information showed faster dynamics (Figure 7C, continuous black line), with new information arriving faster than the peak of the linear prediction (Figure 7C, green line).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing different measures in the model output shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The timing of the increase in information from gating greatly overlapped with the timing of the expected increase in the conditional information following the shift.
source: We found that these greatly overlapped, meaning that the active increase in information produced by gating is timed to match the expected increase in novel information generated by the shift.
evidence: This is shown by the comparison in Figure 7D between experimental and model results.

claim: Gating represents a mechanism that increases information transmission at the expected peak of novel information after a global shift in the image.
source: Given the statistics of natural scenes and the measured noise in bipolar cells, our model indicates that gating represents a mechanism that increases information transmission at the expected peak of novel information after a global shift in the image.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis comparing gating timing to expected information dynamics.

claim: A peripheral shift causes a switch from a code that conserves energy to one of increased information transmission.
source: Our findings indicate that a peripheral shift causes a switch from a code that conserves energy to one of increased information transmission, with higher information transmission occurring at the expected time of higher signal-to-noise ratio and higher information content.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings regarding energy efficiency and information transmission.

claim: The findings reveal the dynamic allocation of energy resources to increase neural activity at times of expected high information content.
source: Our findings reveal the dynamic allocation of energy resources to increase neural activity at times of expected high information content, a principle of adaptation that balances the competing requirements of conserving spikes and transmitting information.
evidence: This is a high-level interpretive claim about the principle underlying the observed phenomena.

claim: An energy-efficient communications channel that carries signals over a range of frequencies should allocate power such that signal power plus noise power is a constant, except for frequencies where noise exceeds a value set by the available power.
source: An energy-efficient communications channel that carries signals over a range of frequencies should allocate power such that signal power plus noise power is a constant, except for frequencies where noise exceeds a value set by the available power (Shannon, 1998; Warland and Rieke, 1999).
evidence: This is a principle from communications theory cited from the literature.

claim: The same water-filling principle applies to efficiently allocate power over time when the noise level dynamically varies.
source: It is less well appreciated in neuroscience that the same water-filling principle applies to efficiently allocate power over time when the noise level dynamically varies as can occur during wireless transmission (Goldsmith and Varaiya, 1997).
evidence: This extends the communications theory principle to the temporal domain, citing relevant literature.

claim: Greater power should be allocated to times of higher SNR according to the water-filling principle.
source: In this case, greater power should be allocated to times of higher SNR.
evidence: This is a consequence of the water-filling principle applied to time-varying signals.

claim: A higher variance signal has a higher SNR in the bipolar cell.
source: Because a higher variance signal has a higher SNR in the bipolar cell (Figure 7A-iii [Ozuysal, 2012]), this principle agrees with our observation that additional spiking is allocated to times of expected high variance of the filtered stimulus (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements cited from previous work and shown in Figure 7A-iii.

claim: Gating occurs at the time when the expected statistics of the central input will change.
source: Our results indicated that gating occurs at the time when the expected statistics of the central input will change.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the timing analysis comparing gating to expected information changes.

claim: Peripheral gating will be important during natural saccadic eye movements.
source: This expectation may arise from the sudden movement of large objects, and we expect that peripheral gating will be important during natural saccadic eye movements.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional role of gating during natural behavior.

claim: Previous results have strongly implicated transient nonlinear peripheral inhibition in suppressing the effects of fixational eye movements on object motion sensitive ganglion cells.
source: Previous results have strongly implicated transient nonlinear peripheral inhibition in suppressing the effects of fixational eye movements on object motion sensitive ganglion cells (Olveczky et al., 2003), and the similar spatial scale of peripheral nonlinear gating and nonlinear inhibition (Figure 6) is consistent with a role of gating in eye movements.
evidence: This claim cites previous literature and connects it to the current findings.

claim: Salamanders and other amphibians have similar fixational drift and optokinetic head movements to mammals.
source: Although salamanders and other amphibians have differences in their eye movements in that they make head saccades to target prey (Manteuffel and Roth, 1993), they have similar fixational drift (Manteuffel et al., 1977) and optokinetic head movements (Manteuffel, 1984) to mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by cited literature on amphibian eye movements.

claim: The property of object motion sensitivity related to fixational eye movements is common to both salamanders and mammals.
source: Accordingly, the property of object motion sensitivity related to fixational eye movements is common to both salamanders and mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of eye movement properties across species.

claim: The basic phenomenon of peripheral retinal excitation has been observed in mammals.
source: Similarly, the basic phenomenon of peripheral retinal excitation has been observed in mammals, and we expect that effects on neural coding we observe here will be similar.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature and makes a prediction about generalizability.

claim: The duration of the ~1 degree global image shifts used is similar to the duration of a ~1 degree saccade in a number of species.
source: The duration of the ~1 degree global image shifts we have used (Figure 1) is one stimulus frame (~30 ms), similar to the duration of a ~1 degree saccade in a number of species, for rabbit, cat and monkey, 20–50 ms (Collewijn and Zuidam, 1977; Evinger et al., 1981; Fuchs and Johns, 1967); humans, ~20 ms (Baloh et al., 1975); and fish, ~70 ms (Easter, 1975).
evidence: This claim compares experimental parameters to natural saccade durations cited from the literature.

claim: The key property is that the timing of the linear filter in the receptive field center is coincident with temporal filtering from the peripheral input.
source: Although larger saccadic eye movements are longer in duration, the key property we find is that the timing of the linear filter in the receptive field center is coincident with temporal filtering from the peripheral input.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about what aspect of the findings is most important for generalization.

claim: Timing signals that indicate a changing stimulus have been observed in other systems that use active sensation, including sniffing in olfaction and whisking in the vibrissae system.
source: Timing signals that indicate a changing stimulus have been observed in other systems that use active sensation, including sniffing in olfaction and whisking in the vibrissae system (Shusterman et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim cites literature on timing signals in other sensory systems.

claim: Because the retina lacks an efferent copy, a signal that the stimulus is changing must be computed from the sensory input.
source: But because the retina lacks such an efferent copy, a signal that the stimulus is changing must be computed from the sensory input.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about retinal circuitry and logical inference.

claim: Inhibitory amacrine cells are known to deliver signals laterally across long distances, and could increase the firing rate through synaptic disinhibition.
source: Inhibitory amacrine cells are known to deliver signals laterally across long distances, and could increase the firing rate through synaptic disinhibition (Barlow et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about retinal circuitry and cited literature.

claim: A similar organization is found in the hippocampus, where a common signal is generated by oscillations in inhibitory neurons.
source: We note that a similar organization is found in the hippocampus, where a common signal is generated by oscillations in inhibitory neurons (Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This claim draws a parallel to another brain system based on cited literature.

claim: Synchronous oscillations between brain regions may perform a similar function of allocating sensitivity to time intervals of greater information content.
source: On the principle that the threshold should be lowered when greater information is expected, synchronous oscillations between brain regions may perform a similar function of allocating sensitivity to time intervals of greater information content.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential function of neural oscillations based on the principles identified in this study.

claim: A high threshold may be efficient in terms of energy, at the expense of the amount of information.
source: A high threshold may be efficient in terms of energy, at the expense of the amount of information (Pitkow and Meister, 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on cited previous work on neural coding efficiency.

claim: A biphasic filter and a threshold may emphasize novelty in natural scenes.
source: A biphasic filter and a threshold may emphasize novelty in natural scenes (Srinivasan et al., 1982), but certain stimuli such as a constant luminance will be rejected.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature and logical inference about filter properties.

claim: An adaptive system may improve information transmission across an entire set of stimuli, but the particular statistic that triggers adaptation may be lost.
source: An adaptive system may improve information transmission across an entire set of stimuli, but the particular statistic that triggers adaptation may be lost.
evidence: This is based on general principles of adaptive coding systems.

claim: Cells can sequentially switch between complementary representations to capture the benefits of both.
source: Our results, however, show that cells can sequentially switch between complementary representations to capture the benefits of both.
evidence: This is a high-level conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about dynamic coding.
